solution.concept_anchor: Devprayag confluence — Ganga naming point
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because Gangotri glacier is universally associated with the Ganga and students who conflate 'glacial source' with 'river origin by name' will choose it.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Gangotri is the glacial source of Bhagirathi, not the point where the river is officially named Ganga.
Eliminate (c): Haridwar is where Ganga descends into the plains — it is a geomorphological transition, not a naming confluence.
Eliminate (d): Rishikesh is upstream of Haridwar and has no confluence role in naming the river.
Confirm (b): At Devprayag, Bhagirathi and Alaknanda merge — the resultant river is called Ganga from this point onward.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits the common conflation of 'glacial origin' with 'river naming'. Students confidently recall 'Ganga originates at Gangotri' — which is true for the glacial source — but the river earns the name Ganga only at Devprayag where Bhagirathi meets Alaknanda. Gangotri is the source of Bhagirathi, one of the two streams that form Ganga. A superficially prepared student will choose (a) without realising the distinction between glacial source and the confluence-based naming convention.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ganga river system has a layered origin: the Bhagirathi stream emerges from Gangotri glacier, while Alaknanda has its own independent course draining from glaciers like Satopanth. The river receives the name 'Ganga' only at Devprayag, where these two streams converge — making Devprayag the legal and geographic naming point of India's national river.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Gangotri is the glacial source of Bhagirathi, one of Ganga's headstreams, not the naming origin of the Ganga river itself.
• Option (b) — Correct: Devprayag is the fifth and final confluence in the Panch Prayag sequence, where Bhagirathi and Alaknanda unite to form the Ganga.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Haridwar marks where the Ganga exits the Shivalik hills and enters the Indo-Gangetic Plains — a geomorphological, not nominative, transition.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Rishikesh lies upstream of Haridwar; the river is already called Ganga at this point.

Value Addition:
• The Panch Prayag are: Vishnuprayag → Nandprayag → Karnaprayag → Rudraprayag → Devprayag (upstream to downstream).
• Alaknanda is longer than Bhagirathi, yet the river is named after Bhagirathi — a classic UPSC trap.
• Devprayag is in Tehri Garhwal district, Uttarakhand.

solution.concept_anchor: Panch Prayag tributary sequence

statement_analysis.statement: The Pindar river joins the Alaknanda at Karnaprayag.
statement_analysis.reason: Karnaprayag is the confluence of Pindar (from Pindari glacier) and Alaknanda — this is the third prayag in the upstream-to-downstream sequence.

statement_analysis.statement: The Mandakini river joins the Alaknanda at Rudraprayag.
statement_analysis.reason: Rudraprayag is where Mandakini (originating near Kedarnath) meets Alaknanda — this is the fourth prayag in the sequence.

statement_analysis.statement: The Nandakini river joins the Alaknanda at Vishnuprayag.
statement_analysis.reason: Nandakini joins at Nandprayag, not Vishnuprayag. At Vishnuprayag, the Dhauliganga merges with Alaknanda.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who know both Statements 1 and 2 are correct might doubt one of them under exam pressure and choose a partial option.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 3 first — Nandakini joins at Nandprayag; Vishnuprayag receives the Dhauliganga. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 1 — Pindar at Karnaprayag is a well-established fact. Statement 1 is correct.
Verify Statement 2 — Mandakini at Rudraprayag is confirmed. Statement 2 is correct.
With Statements 1 and 2 correct and Statement 3 incorrect, the answer is (c): 1 and 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is an entity-swap: Nandakini is correctly associated with the Nandprayag confluence, but the statement reassigns it to Vishnuprayag — the very first prayag. Students who recall 'Nandakini is one of the Panch Prayag tributaries' without remembering the precise pairing will accept Statement 3 as true, leading them to choose (d) instead of (c).
solution.final_explanation:
The Panch Prayag are five sacred confluences along the Alaknanda river in Uttarakhand, proceeding downstream: Vishnuprayag (Dhauliganga + Alaknanda), Nandprayag (Nandakini + Alaknanda), Karnaprayag (Pindar + Alaknanda), Rudraprayag (Mandakini + Alaknanda), and finally Devprayag (Bhagirathi + Alaknanda = Ganga).

• Statement 1 — Correct: Pindar river indeed joins at Karnaprayag; it originates from the Pindari glacier in Kumaon.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Mandakini joins at Rudraprayag; the 2013 Kedarnath disaster affected the Mandakini valley.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Nandakini joins at Nandprayag; Vishnuprayag is the confluence of Dhauliganga with Alaknanda.

Value Addition:
• Memory aid for sequence: Very Nice Kids Ride Downstream (Vishnuprayag, Nandprayag, Karnaprayag, Rudraprayag, Devprayag).
• Tributaries in order: Dhauliganga, Nandakini, Pindar, Mandakini, Bhagirathi.
• Rudraprayag district is named after the confluence — same district as Kedarnath shrine.

solution.concept_anchor: Antecedent drainage — all major Himalayan rivers

statement_analysis.statement: Antecedent drainage refers to rivers that developed their courses after the uplift of the mountain ranges through which they flow.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the opposite of the correct definition. Antecedent rivers are older than the mountain ranges — they maintained their original course as the mountains rose around them through tectonic uplift.

statement_analysis.statement: Among the major Himalayan rivers, only the Ganga tributaries exhibit antecedent drainage — the Indus and Brahmaputra follow a different drainage pattern.
statement_analysis.reason: All three major Himalayan river systems — Indus, Ganga tributaries, and Brahmaputra — are antecedent rivers. The trap here is the word 'only', which artificially restricts the scope.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 1 as wrong might accept Statement 2 as partially true (knowing Ganga is antecedent) without verifying the 'only' qualifier.
elimination_logic: Examine Statement 1: antecedent drainage means rivers pre-date the mountains, not post-date them. Statement 1 reverses the definition — it is incorrect.
Examine Statement 2: the word 'only' limits antecedent nature to Ganga tributaries. Indus and Brahmaputra are equally antecedent — Statement 2 is also incorrect.
Both statements are incorrect, so the answer is (d): Neither 1 nor 2.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses the scope-extension trap via 'only'. A student who knows Ganga tributaries are antecedent rivers will treat the first part as true without scrutinising the exclusion of Indus and Brahmaputra. In reality, the Indus gorges near Gilgit and the Brahmaputra's Yarlung Tsangpo canyon are among the world's deepest — both classic examples of antecedent drainage predating Himalayan uplift.
solution.final_explanation:
Antecedent drainage describes rivers that are geologically older than the mountain ranges they traverse. As the Himalayas rose due to the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates, these rivers maintained their pre-existing courses and cut progressively deeper gorges through the rising mountains.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The definition is inverted. Antecedent rivers pre-date the mountains, not the other way around. This is why the Gandak, Kosi, and other tributaries cut deep gorges through the Himalayas.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Indus (Gilgit gorge), the Ganga tributaries, and the Brahmaputra (Namcha Barwa gorge) are all antecedent. Restricting antecedence to 'only Ganga tributaries' is factually wrong.

Value Addition:
• Consequent rivers (e.g., most Peninsular rivers) follow the slope of the land — they developed after the terrain was formed.
• The Brahmaputra's gorge near Namcha Barwa is one of the world's deepest — classic antecedent evidence.
• Superimposed drainage occurs when a river flowing on a softer rock layer cuts through and exposes underlying harder rock, maintaining its original course.

statement_analysis.statement: Chambal — joins Yamuna in Uttar Pradesh after draining through Rajasthan

statement_analysis.statement: Betwa — originates in the Vindhyan highlands and joins Yamuna at Hamirpur (UP)
statement_analysis.reason: Betwa rises from the Vindhyan ranges near Bhopal (MP) and meets the Yamuna at Hamirpur, UP — both the origin and confluence location are correct.

statement_analysis.statement: Ken — joins Yamuna at Allahabad (Prayagraj), downstream of the Ganga-Yamuna confluence
statement_analysis.reason: Ken joins Yamuna at Chilla in UP (near Banda), not at Prayagraj. Prayagraj is where Yamuna meets Ganga, not where Ken meets Yamuna.

statement_analysis.statement: Sind — a right-bank tributary of Yamuna originating in the Vindhyan plateau of Madhya Pradesh
statement_analysis.reason: The Sind (also Sindh) river rises near Vidisha in MP and is indeed a right-bank Peninsular tributary of Yamuna, joining it in UP.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is a strong distractor because the Chambal, Betwa, and Sind pairings are all accurate, and students may miss the subtle error in Ken's confluence location.
elimination_logic: Verify Chambal: drains through Rajasthan, joins Yamuna in UP — correct.
Verify Betwa: Vindhyan origin, Hamirpur confluence — correct.
Verify Ken: joins Yamuna at Chilla (Banda district), NOT at Prayagraj — this pairing is incorrect; Prayagraj is where Yamuna meets Ganga.
Verify Sind: Vindhyan plateau origin, right-bank tributary of Yamuna — correct. Three pairs are correct, so the answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Ken pairing plants Prayagraj as the confluence location — a plausible-sounding error because Prayagraj is the most famous confluence on the Yamuna (where it meets Ganga). A student who knows Ken is a Yamuna tributary but hasn't memorised its precise confluence point will accept 'Prayagraj' as credible and mark all four as correct, choosing (d) instead of (c).
solution.final_explanation:
The Yamuna receives several Peninsular (right-bank) tributaries originating in the Vindhyan and Bundelkhand regions — these are non-glacial rivers whose flows are largely monsoon-dependent and contribute significantly to Yamuna's water volume.

| River | Correct Status |
|---|---|
| Chambal | Correct — joins Yamuna in Etawah, UP |
| Betwa | Correct — joins at Hamirpur, UP |
| Ken | Incorrect — joins at Chilla (Banda), NOT Prayagraj |
| Sind | Correct — Vindhyan origin, right-bank tributary |

Only three pairs are correctly described, making (c) the answer.

• Chambal, Betwa, Ken, and Sind collectively form the drainage backbone of the Bundelkhand plateau.
• Ken-Betwa interlinking is the first project under the National River Linking Project to receive all clearances — it passes through Panna Tiger Reserve.
• The right bank of Yamuna drains the Peninsular plateau; the left bank drains the Himalayan foothills (Hindon, Rishiganga, Sengar).

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) swaps Gandak's confluence to Patna city proper; students who know Gandak joins Ganga in Bihar but haven't memorised 'Hajipur' specifically will choose (b).
elimination_logic: Kosi joins Ganga near Kursela (not Patna) — this eliminates any option that places Kosi at Patna.

Son joins Ganga near Patna (Arrah/Dinapur area) on the right bank — confirm B-3.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap places Kosi's confluence at Patna — a highly memorable city — when it actually joins at Kursela in Katihar district. Students who recall 'Kosi is the Sorrow of Bihar' and associate it with major Bihar cities will anchor it to Patna. Similarly, Hajipur (Gandak's confluence) and Saran (Ghaghara's confluence) are less prominently recalled, creating multiple simultaneous confusion points.
solution.final_explanation:
Several major Himalayan tributaries join the Ganga across the Bihar plains. The precise confluence locations are critical exam facts because UPSC frequently tests geographic precision over generic regional knowledge.

Correct matches:
• A (Gandak) — 2 (Hajipur, opposite Patna across the river): Gandak, also called Narayani in Nepal, joins at Hajipur in Vaishali district.

• C (Ghaghara) — 1 (Saran district): Ghaghara, the largest tributary by discharge, joins in Saran district of Bihar.
• D (Kosi) — 4 (Kursela, Katihar district): Kosi joins far east of Patna near Kursela — not at Patna as commonly misremembered.

The trap pairing is D-Kosi with 'Patna' (option 3), which conflates the river's Bihar association with an incorrect confluence city.

• Ghaghara > Yamuna in discharge; Yamuna > Ghaghara in length — a frequently tested contrast.
• Hajipur is in Vaishali district; it hosts Asia's largest cattle fair (Sonepur Mela) at the Gandak-Ganga confluence.
• Kursela is in Katihar district — note this for locational precision questions.

solution.concept_anchor: Yamuna longest tributary vs. Ghaghara largest by discharge
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because both A and R are factually true, and students who do not scrutinise the causal link will assume discharge determines naming precedence and choose (a).
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yamuna is indeed the longest tributary of Ganga by total river length. A is correct.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Ghaghara does carry greater discharge than Yamuna, especially during monsoon. R is correct.
Step 3: Does R explain A? — Ghaghara's higher discharge does not explain why Yamuna is longer in length. Length and discharge are independent hydrological parameters. R does not explain A.
A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A → correct_option is (b). Wait — re-checking: the option pattern gives (b) as 'Both correct, R not the explanation'. Correct answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Both the assertion and reason are individually true facts, making this a classic Type-B assertion-reason trap. Students who verify both as true will reflexively choose (a), assuming the longer river would naturally have less discharge — without pausing to ask whether discharge volume is what determines a river's length classification. The causal link is absent: length is determined by geographic course distance, while discharge depends on catchment area, snowmelt, and precipitation patterns.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests two independent hydrological parameters: river length and river discharge.

Assertion (A): The Yamuna is the longest tributary of the Ganga, with a total length of approximately 1,376 km from Yamunotri to Prayagraj. This is factually correct.

Reason (R): The Ghaghara (Karnali) carries the largest volume of water (discharge) among all Ganga tributaries — its catchment in Nepal and Tibet receives heavy precipitation and snowmelt. This is also factually correct.

Causal relationship: The Yamuna's greater length is a function of its geographic course — it originates in the northwestern Himalayas and follows a long southeastward arc through the Gangetic Plain. The Ghaghara's higher discharge is determined by its larger catchment area and Himalayan snowmelt inputs. These are independent parameters; one does not explain the other. Hence (b) is correct.

Value Addition:
• Yamuna length ≈ 1,376 km; Ghaghara length ≈ 1,080 km — Yamuna is longer.
• Ghaghara discharge often exceeds Yamuna's by 2–3 times during peak monsoon.
• Triveni Sangam at Prayagraj — Ganga, Yamuna, and the mythical Saraswati — is a critical GS-I cultural geography point.

solution.concept_anchor: Kosi river management — treaty and disaster timeline
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students who remember '1966' as a Kosi treaty year may place it before 1954 if they confuse it with a different agreement, disrupting the sequence.
elimination_logic: The Kosi Barrage at Bhimnagar was built under the 1954 India-Nepal Treaty — this is the earliest event in the sequence.
The Kosi Treaty was revised/supplemented in 1966 — this follows 1954.
The 2008 Kosi flood disaster (Kusaha breach) is the most recent event — it must come last.
Correct sequence: 1954 Treaty → 1966 Revision → 2008 Flood disaster = option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal trap lies between 1954 and 1966 — both are real treaty years associated with the Kosi. Students who remember only one date may place the sequence incorrectly. Option (a) inverts the treaty years, while option (c) places the 2008 disaster before the 1966 revision — both are plausible errors for partially prepared students who know the events but not their precise sequence.
solution.final_explanation:
The Kosi river management history involves a sequence of diplomatic and disaster events spanning over five decades.

Correct sequence:
1. India-Nepal Treaty on Kosi (1954): established the framework for the Kosi Barrage at Bhimnagar, Nepal — a joint flood-control and irrigation project.
2. Kosi Treaty revision (1966): modified and supplemented the original 1954 agreement to address operational issues and water-sharing details.
3. Kusaha embankment breach, 2008: the eastern embankment in Nepal's Sunsari district was breached, causing catastrophic flooding across Bihar — one of India's worst recent flood disasters.

Option (a) inverts 1954 and 1966; option (c) places 2008 before 1966; option (d) puts 2008 in the middle.

Value Addition:
• Kosi has shifted ~120 km westward over 200 years — among the world's highest river avulsion rates.
• 'Sorrow of Bihar' — Kosi; 'Sorrow of Bengal' — Damodar; 'Sorrow of Assam' — Brahmaputra (all exam-relevant).
• Kosi joins the Ganga near Kursela in Katihar district, Bihar — not at Patna.

solution.concept_anchor: National Chambal Sanctuary — species and river order
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because the Ganga is the ultimate receiver of Chambal's water and students may associate the sanctuary's biodiversity with the main stem rather than its actual tributary status.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a sanctuary on a river famous for gharial and Gangetic dolphin — these are specifically associated with the Chambal.
Eliminate (a): Son river flows through central MP but is not known for the gharial sanctuary or ravine topography in this context.
Eliminate (b): the Ganga main stem runs through UP and Bihar; the scenario's river joins a major tributary before reaching Ganga.
Eliminate (c): Betwa does not host a major gharial sanctuary and flows through Bundelkhand without the ravine-dacoity association.
Confirm (d): All features — Vindhyan origin, ravines, gharial sanctuary, joining Yamuna (not Ganga directly) — precisely fit the Chambal.
solution.final_explanation:
The Chambal is India's most ecologically significant Peninsular tributary in the Ganga system. It originates in the Janapav hills of the Vindhyan ranges (MP), flows through Rajasthan, forms the MP-Rajasthan border, and joins the Yamuna in Etawah district of UP — making it a second-order tributary of the Ganga (tributary of a tributary).

The National Chambal Sanctuary (also called Gharial Sanctuary) spans MP, Rajasthan, and UP — one of the last refuges for:
• Gharial (Critically Endangered)
• Gangetic river dolphin (Endangered)
• Red-crowned roof turtle

The ravines of the Chambal — caused by severe land degradation — are historically associated with dacoity (banditry). Kota Barrage in Rajasthan diverts Chambal water for irrigation.

Option (d) is correct because the river joins the Yamuna (not Ganga directly), originates in the Vindhyan highlands, and hosts the gharial sanctuary — all pointing uniquely to the Chambal.

Value Addition:
• Chambal is a second-order tributary of Ganga (Chambal → Yamuna → Ganga).
• The Chambal ravines cover approximately 4,000 sq km across MP, UP, and Rajasthan.
• Kota Barrage is used for the Rajasthan Canal (Indira Gandhi Canal) linkage system.

solution.concept_anchor: Second-order vs. first-order Ganga tributaries
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because Son is a less prominent right-bank tributary and students may mistakenly think it joins via Yamuna like Chambal, when it joins the Ganga main stem directly.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap works by grouping four Peninsular rivers together. Students who know all four originate from the Vindhyan/Peninsular region may class them together as 'Peninsular tributaries of the Ganga system' without distinguishing between first-order (direct Ganga) and second-order (via Yamuna) tributaries. Son is directly a right-bank tributary of the Ganga, while Betwa, Chambal, and Ken all join the Yamuna first.

This question tests the order of tributary relationships within the Ganga drainage basin.

• Betwa — joins Yamuna at Hamirpur (second-order Ganga tributary)
• Chambal — joins Yamuna in Etawah (second-order Ganga tributary)
• Ken — joins Yamuna at Chilla, Banda (second-order Ganga tributary)
• Son — joins the Ganga main stem near Patna on the right bank (first-order Ganga tributary)

Betwa, Chambal, and Ken share the common attribute of being tributaries of Yamuna (and hence second-order tributaries of Ganga). Son is the odd one out — it flows northeast from Amarkantak and joins the Ganga directly.

• Son is the second largest right-bank tributary of the Ganga after Yamuna.
• Amarkantak plateau is the triple watershed for Son (northeast), Narmada (west), and Johilla rivers.

solution.concept_anchor: Hooghly as westernmost distributary — not main Ganga channel

statement_analysis.statement: The Hooghly is a distributary of the Ganga and is the westernmost major distributary of the Ganga delta system in India.
statement_analysis.reason: Hooghly (also called Bhagirathi in its upper reach) is a distributary — it branches off from the Ganga near Farakka/Murshidabad and flows south through West Bengal. It is the westernmost significant distributary.

statement_analysis.statement: The Farakka Barrage was constructed primarily to regulate flooding in Bihar and to provide water to Bangladesh during the lean season.
statement_analysis.reason: Farakka Barrage was built to divert Ganga waters into the Hooghly to flush siltation and maintain Kolkata Port's navigability — not primarily for flood control in Bihar or water supply to Bangladesh. Providing water to Bangladesh was a contentious side-effect, not the primary purpose.

solution.strong_distractor: a — this IS the correct answer. The strong distractor is (c): students who misread Statement 2 as mostly correct (Bangladesh + lean season being real issues) may choose (c) thinking both are individually correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Hooghly is a distributary (branches off, does not join Ganga) — correct. It is the westernmost — correct. Statement 1 is true.

Evaluate Statement 2: Farakka's primary purpose is to maintain Hooghly's navigability for Kolkata Port by diverting silt-flushing flows — not Bihar flood control or Bangladesh supply. Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option (c) applies. Correct answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 conflates multiple Farakka-related issues: the Bangladesh water dispute, Bihar flooding, and the actual primary purpose (Kolkata port navigability). Students aware of the India-Bangladesh Ganga Water Treaty 1996 and Bangladesh's complaints about reduced downstream flow may mistakenly accept 'providing water to Bangladesh during lean season' as the stated purpose, when it is actually a treaty obligation — not the construction rationale.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ganga delta distributary system and the Farakka Barrage are two frequently tested topics that appear simple but contain critical factual traps.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Hooghly is a westward-branching distributary of the Ganga. It is fed by a diversion at Farakka and flows through Kolkata to the Bay of Bengal. It is the only navigable distributary and the westernmost in the Indian portion of the delta.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Farakka Barrage (completed 1975) was built specifically to divert Ganga water into the Hooghly to flush accumulated silt and maintain the navigability of Kolkata Port. Bihar flood control and Bangladesh water supply were not its primary objectives.

Value Addition:
• The Ganga Water Treaty (1996) — a 30-year agreement — allocates Farakka flows between India and Bangladesh during January–May (lean season).
• Hooghly is sometimes called 'Bhagirathi' in its upper reaches near Murshidabad.
• The Padma river in Bangladesh is the continuation of the main Ganga channel after it crosses the border.

solution.concept_anchor: Bhangar — kankar nodules, old alluvium distinction
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because Khadar is the other alluvial zone and students who know 'Khadar vs. Bhangar' often mix up which one contains kankar nodules.
elimination_logic: Kankar nodules (calcium carbonate concretions) are a defining characteristic of older alluvial deposits — this rules out Khadar (new, regularly renewed alluvium).
Bhabar is the porous gravel zone at the Himalayan foothills — no alluvial deposits with kankar.
Terai is the waterlogged belt south of Bhabar — not an alluvial zone known for kankar.
Bhangar (old alluvium, elevated terrace land) contains kankar nodules — confirm (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap places Khadar in the blank. Since Khadar and Bhangar are the two most discussed alluvial sub-types, students who recall 'one of them has kankar' but mix up which one will confidently choose (a). Khadar is the newer, more fertile alluvium regularly deposited by floods — it does not have kankar. Bhangar is the older, elevated terrace alluvium that does contain kankar.
solution.final_explanation:
The Indo-Gangetic alluvial plain is differentiated into zones based on age and composition of deposits.

• Option (a) Khadar — Incorrect: Khadar is newer alluvium, deposited regularly by river floods. It is more fertile and found in the active floodplains. It does not contain kankar.
• Option (b) Bhabar — Incorrect: Bhabar is a narrow porous gravel belt at the foothills where rivers deposit coarse material and streams disappear underground.
• Option (c) Bhangar — Correct: Bhangar is the older alluvium, forming elevated terrace areas away from the floodplain. It contains calcium carbonate concretions called kankar and is less fertile than Khadar.
• Option (d) Terai — Incorrect: Terai is the waterlogged, marshy belt south of Bhabar where underground streams re-emerge. It is not an alluvial terrace.

Value Addition:
• North-to-south sequence: Shivaliks → Bhabar → Terai → Bhangar → Khadar → Delta.
• Bhabar: streams submerge; Terai: streams re-emerge — this sequential logic is a common UPSC trap.
• Doabs (inter-fluve areas) are typically covered by Bhangar soils.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges 'Ganga system' with 'Ganga main stem'. Damodar is indeed part of the Ganga drainage basin, but it joins the Hooghly — a distributary, not the main river. Students who know 'Damodar is a Ganga system river' will accept the pairing without distinguishing between joining the main channel versus a distributary. solution.final_explanation:

• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: Damodar joins the Hooghly (a distributary), not the Ganga main stem. This is the answer.

• Damodar basin: Dhanbad, Bokaro, Durgapur — India's industrial heartland.

solution.concept_anchor: Ganga declared National River — 2008, policy significance only

statement_analysis.statement: The Ganga Action Plan was launched in 1985 to address industrial and sewage pollution along the river.
statement_analysis.reason: The Ganga Action Plan (Phase I) was launched in 1986, not 1985. The temporal swap by one year is a classic UPSC precision trap.

statement_analysis.statement: The declaration of Ganga as India's 'National River' in 2008 carries policy significance but does not confer any formal constitutional or legal status on the river.
statement_analysis.reason: The Ganga was declared the National River in 2008 — but this was an executive/policy declaration, not backed by constitutional amendment or specific legislation, giving it symbolic rather than enforceable legal status.

statement_analysis.statement: The Namami Gange Programme (2014) subsumed and reconstituted the National Ganga River Basin Authority into the National Mission for Clean Ganga.
statement_analysis.reason: Under Namami Gange, the NGRBA (constituted under the Environment Protection Act, 1986) was restructured and the NMCG was designated as the implementing body — this institutional restructuring is a documented feature of the programme.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) '2 and 3 only' is a strong distractor because students who know Statements 2 and 3 are true but doubt Statement 1's year (guessing 1985 might be correct) may choose (a) while actually arriving at the right answer for the wrong reason — but (a) says 2 and 3 only, which IS correct here. Re-check: correct_option is (b): 2 and 3 only. Wait — (a) is '1 and 2 only' and (b) is '2 and 3 only'. With Statements 2 and 3 correct and Statement 1 incorrect, correct_option is (b).
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: GAP Phase I was launched in 1986 (not 1985) — Statement 1 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 2: The 2008 National River declaration is executive/policy, not constitutional — Statement 2 is correct.
Verify Statement 3: NGRBA was reconstituted as NMCG under Namami Gange — Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statements 2 and 3 are correct → answer is (b): 2 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 1985 vs. 1986 trap is a one-year temporal swap — a signature UPSC technique. The Ganga Action Plan is so frequently cited in environmental discourse that students hardcode it without verifying the exact launch year. 1985 feels plausible because major environmental legislation (like the Environment Protection Act) came in 1986, creating a mental association. The GAP was actually launched by Rajiv Gandhi's government in 1986.
solution.final_explanation:
India's effort to clean the Ganga spans four decades of institutional evolution.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Ganga Action Plan Phase I was launched in 1986 (not 1985). It was largely unsuccessful due to poor sewage treatment infrastructure, low public participation, and fragmented institutional responsibility.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The 'National River' declaration for Ganga in 2008 (under Manmohan Singh's government) is a policy milestone without constitutional backing. It created the National Ganga River Basin Authority but did not give the river enforceable legal personhood.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Namami Gange (2014) with a ₹20,000 crore outlay replaced the fragmented earlier approach. The NGRBA was reconstituted as the NMCG under the Environment Protection Act framework.

Value Addition:
• Kanpur tanneries (chromium effluents) are among the most cited industrial pollution sources on the Ganga.
• Ganga is the only river in India to be declared a 'National River'.
• Allahabad High Court (2017) declared Ganga and Yamuna as living entities — later stayed by the Supreme Court.

solution.concept_anchor: Glacier retreat — short-term flow increase vs. long-term flow reduction
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — In the short term, accelerated glacier melting does increase river flow (meltwater surge). A is factually correct.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — The Gangotri glacier is indeed one of the fastest-receding glaciers in the Himalayas. R is factually correct.
Step 3: Does R explain A? — Gangotri's recession rate explains WHY meltwater is increasing currently — this is a direct causal link. R does correctly explain A.
A correct + R correct + R explains A → correct_option is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap targets students who know the long-term impact of glacier retreat (reduced river flow) and assume that must be the assertion. The assertion here is specifically about the SHORT-TERM effect (increased meltwater = higher flow), which is the opposite. Students who conflate short-term and long-term impacts will find the assertion 'wrong' and choose (d). The reason correctly points to Gangotri recession as the cause of current meltwater surge — making (a) the answer.
solution.final_explanation:
Himalayan glacier retreat has a dual and apparently contradictory impact on river hydrology — a key UPSC differentiation point.

Assertion (A): In the current period, accelerated melting of Himalayan glaciers is contributing to higher-than-historical river flows in glacially-fed rivers like Bhagirathi and Mandakini. This is the SHORT-TERM meltwater surge effect. It is correct.

Reason (R): The Gangotri glacier, which feeds the Bhagirathi (headstream of Ganga), has been receding at an accelerating rate — among the fastest in the Himalayas. This is documented by the Geological Survey of India. It is correct.

R explains A directly: Gangotri's accelerated recession is releasing excess meltwater that boosts current river flows — the causal link is valid. Answer is (a).

Value Addition:
• Long-term (post-glacier disappearance): rivers will have significantly reduced dry-season flow, threatening water security for hundreds of millions.
• GLOF risk increases as glaciers retreat and moraine-dammed lakes form — Kedarnath 2013 and Chamoli 2021 are examples.
• Gangotri has receded over 22 km since 1780; current recession rate is approximately 22 metres per year.

solution.concept_anchor: Ramganga — tributary of Ganga, not Yamuna
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because Ramganga originates in Uttarakhand (like many Yamuna tributaries) and students may automatically associate Uttarakhand-origin rivers with the Yamuna system.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (b): Ramganga originates in Pauri Garhwal and flows southeast — it does not join the Yamuna. It joins the Ganga near Kannauj in UP.
Eliminate (c): Ramganga is not a tributary of the Ghaghara; Ghaghara originates from Tibet and flows through Nepal.
Eliminate (d): Ramganga does not join the Gandak; Gandak originates near Mustang.
Confirm (a): Ramganga joins the Ganga near Kannauj (UP) — it is a left-bank tributary of Ganga.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap exploits the geographic association: Ramganga originates in Uttarakhand's Pauri Garhwal, the same broad region as several Yamuna headstreams. Students who categorise all Uttarakhand-origin rivers as Yamuna tributaries will choose (b). However, Ramganga's course bends east, not southwest, and it joins the Ganga — not the Yamuna — near Kannauj.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ramganga is a significant but often overlooked Himalayan tributary of the Ganga.

• Option (a) — Correct: Ramganga joins the Ganga near Kannauj in Uttar Pradesh. It is a left-bank tributary originating in Pauri Garhwal, Uttarakhand. The Kalagarh Dam on Ramganga forms the reservoir adjacent to Jim Corbett National Park.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Ramganga does not join the Yamuna. Despite its Uttarakhand origin, its course takes it eastward into the Ganga, not southwestward to the Yamuna.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Ghaghara (Karnali) is a separate, much larger river originating from Tibet/Nepal — Ramganga is not its tributary.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Gandak originates near Mustang (Nepal); Ramganga is entirely separate.

Value Addition:
• Jim Corbett National Park (est. 1936) is India's oldest national park — located in the Ramganga river basin in Nainital/Pauri Garhwal districts.
• Project Tiger was launched at Corbett in 1973 — the Ramganga reservoir provides critical habitat.

solution.concept_anchor: Gomti joins Ganga — Ghaggar-Hakra is inland drainage

statement_analysis.statement: The Gomti river, which flows through Lucknow, is a tributary of the Yamuna river.
statement_analysis.reason: Gomti is a left-bank tributary of the Ganga (joining near Varanasi/Ghazipur), not of the Yamuna. Despite flowing westward through Lucknow — a city many associate with Yamuna influence — Gomti drains into the Ganga.

statement_analysis.statement: The Ghaggar-Hakra is a seasonal river system that drains into the Ganga near Haridwar after collecting flows from Punjab and Haryana.
statement_analysis.reason: The Ghaggar-Hakra is an inland drainage river — it does not join the Ganga. It loses itself in the Thar Desert in Rajasthan. It is an entirely separate drainage system unconnected to the Ganga basin.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) '1 only' is a strong distractor because Statement 1 (Gomti as Yamuna tributary) feels plausible to students who associate Lucknow with UP's Yamuna-adjacent geography.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: Gomti joins the Ganga near Varanasi/Ghazipur — NOT the Yamuna. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Check Statement 2: Ghaggar-Hakra does not join the Ganga; it is an inland drainage river that dissipates in the Thar Desert. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Both statements are incorrect — but the question asks which are NOT correct, so both qualify. Answer is (c): Both 1 and 2.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses a conflation trap — it associates Ghaggar-Hakra with the Ganga system by inventing a confluence near Haridwar. Students aware that Ghaggar flows through Punjab/Haryana might accept the 'Haridwar' claim without scrutiny, since Haridwar is where the Ganga enters the plains. In reality, Ghaggar-Hakra is one of India's notable inland drainage rivers, draining neither into the Ganga nor the Indus system — it evaporates in the Rajasthan desert.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests two common geographic misconceptions about rivers flowing through north Indian plains.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Gomti originates from Gomat Taal (a lake near Pilibhit, UP) — it is not glacier-fed. It flows through Lucknow and joins the Ganga near Ghazipur/Varanasi as a left-bank tributary. Students confuse it with Yamuna because Lucknow lies in the Yamuna-Ganga doab region.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Ghaggar-Hakra (Punjab → Haryana → Rajasthan) is a classic inland drainage river — it never reaches any major river. It disappears into the Thar Desert near Suratgarh. Some scholars identify it with the ancient Saraswati river of the Harappan civilisation.

Value Addition:
• Ghaggar-Hakra is sometimes called 'Sarsuti' in Punjab — another name linked to Saraswati identification debates.
• Gomti's origin (Gomat Taal, Pilibhit) makes it entirely plains-originating — unusual among left-bank Ganga tributaries.
• Ghaggar flooding in Ambala/Hisar is a current-affairs urban flood concern unrelated to the Ganga system.

solution.concept_anchor: Teesta joins Brahmaputra in Bangladesh — not Ganga directly

statement_analysis.statement: The Teesta river originates from Tso Lhamo lake in Sikkim and flows through North Bengal before entering Bangladesh.
statement_analysis.reason: Tso Lhamo (North Sikkim) is the documented glacial lake origin of the Teesta. The river flows through Sikkim, enters West Bengal (Darjeeling, Jalpaiguri), and then crosses into Bangladesh — all correct.

statement_analysis.statement: In Bangladesh, the Teesta merges with the Padma river, which is the main channel of the Ganga after it crosses the international border.
statement_analysis.reason: The Teesta joins the Brahmaputra (called Jamuna in Bangladesh) — not the Padma (Ganga). The Padma and Jamuna are distinct rivers in Bangladesh, though they eventually merge downstream near Chandpur.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know Teesta is part of the broader 'Ganga-Brahmaputra system' may accept Statement 2 without checking whether Teesta joins Padma or Jamuna specifically.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Tso Lhamo origin and the Sikkim → North Bengal → Bangladesh route are all correct. Statement 1 is true.
Verify Statement 2: Teesta joins the Jamuna (Brahmaputra) in Bangladesh, not the Padma (Ganga main channel). Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap in Statement 2 contains one accurate element (Padma is the Ganga in Bangladesh) embedded in a false claim (Teesta joining Padma). Students who know Padma = Ganga may accept the statement without verifying which river Teesta actually joins. In Bangladesh's river geography, Padma (Ganga) and Jamuna (Brahmaputra) are distinct rivers until they meet at Aricha/Goalanda — and Teesta meets the Jamuna, not the Padma.
solution.final_explanation:
The Teesta river's path and final confluence require precision that goes beyond knowing it is 'part of the Ganga-Brahmaputra system'.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Tso Lhamo (altitude ~5,330 m) in North Sikkim is the origin. The river flows south through Sikkim, enters West Bengal (Darjeeling hills and Terai), and crosses into Bangladesh near Mekhliganj.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: In Bangladesh, the Teesta merges with the Jamuna (the Bangladeshi name for the Brahmaputra), not the Padma. Padma is the Ganga/Ganges after crossing the border. The Teesta-Jamuna confluence occurs in Gaibandha district of Bangladesh.

Value Addition:
• India-Bangladesh Teesta water sharing dispute: a 2011 draft agreement was not signed because West Bengal withheld consent — a rare sub-federal veto in treaty-making.
• Sikkim flash floods 2023: South Lhonak Lake GLOF devastated the Teesta valley, breaching Chungthang Dam.
• Teesta is critical for irrigation in North Bengal's tea gardens and the Teesta Barrage Project.

solution.concept_anchor: Ganga-Brahmaputra delta — largest delta in the world
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because the Mekong delta in Southeast Asia is one of the world's most prominent deltas and students who confuse 'largest' with 'most fertile' or 'most populated' may choose it.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The Nile delta is large and historically significant but covers approximately 24,000 sq km — smaller than the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta (~59,000 sq km).
Eliminate (c): The Mekong delta in Vietnam is ecologically significant but much smaller in area than the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta.
Eliminate (d): The Amazon has a river mouth but does not form a conventional delta — it forms an estuary with tidal influence.
Confirm (b): The Ganga-Brahmaputra delta (~59,000 sq km) is the largest river delta in the world, shared between India and Bangladesh.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) — the Nile delta — is a plausible fabrication in this context because the Nile delta is one of the world's oldest civilisational river deltas and students with broad geographic knowledge often recall it as 'the largest'. The Ganga-Brahmaputra delta's claim to 'largest' is under-emphasised in general education, making the Nile a credible-sounding trap for well-read candidates.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ganga-Brahmaputra delta is the world's largest river delta, covering approximately 59,000 sq km across India (West Bengal) and Bangladesh. It is formed by the combined sediment deposits of the Ganga and Brahmaputra systems into the Bay of Bengal.

• Option (a) Nile delta — Incorrect: The Nile delta covers approximately 24,000 sq km — significant but not the largest. It is historically associated with ancient Egyptian civilisation.
• Option (b) Ganga-Brahmaputra delta — Correct: At ~59,000 sq km, it is the world's largest delta. It hosts the Sundarbans — the world's largest mangrove ecosystem, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and Ramsar wetland.
• Option (c) Mekong delta — Incorrect: The Mekong delta (Vietnam/Cambodia) is ecologically vital but considerably smaller in area.
• Option (d) Amazon river mouth — Incorrect: The Amazon forms an estuary rather than a classic delta; it lacks the depositional structure characteristic of deltas.

Value Addition:
• Sagar Island (West Bengal) is where the Ganga meets the Bay of Bengal — the terminal point of the river.
• The Sundarbans is a shared biosphere reserve between India and Bangladesh.
• The Farakka Barrage was built to maintain Hooghly's navigability within this delta system.

solution.concept_anchor: Indo-Gangetic aquifer — regional differentiation, arsenic contamination

statement_analysis.statement: Satellite-based gravimetric data has revealed a significant and accelerating depletion of groundwater in the northwestern portions of the Indo-Gangetic Plain, particularly in Punjab, Haryana, and western Uttar Pradesh.
statement_analysis.reason: NASA's GRACE satellite mission documented rapid groundwater depletion in NW India's agriculturally intensive zones — one of the fastest rates globally, driven by paddy-wheat cultivation using tube wells.

statement_analysis.statement: Arsenic contamination in groundwater of the lower Ganga plain (Bihar and West Bengal) is primarily caused by industrial discharge from upstream manufacturing zones.
statement_analysis.reason: Arsenic contamination in lower Ganga Plain groundwater is geogenic in origin — it results from natural weathering and reduction of arsenic-bearing iron oxyhydroxide minerals in alluvial sediments, not from industrial discharge.

statement_analysis.statement: The Indo-Gangetic Plain aquifer system is characterised by uniform groundwater availability across all sub-regions.
statement_analysis.reason: The aquifer system is highly heterogeneous: overexploited in the upper doab (NW India) and waterlogged in lower Bihar — the opposite of uniform availability. The 'uniform' qualifier makes this statement false.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) '1 and 3 only' is a strong distractor because Statement 3's authoritative language ('uniform… across all sub-regions') sounds academic and students may accept it without recognising the scope-extension fallacy.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: GRACE satellite data confirming NW India groundwater depletion is well-documented — Statement 1 is correct.
Verify Statement 2: Arsenic in Bihar/WB groundwater is geogenic (natural mineral release), not industrial — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: The aquifer is not uniform — NW India is overexploited while lower Bihar is waterlogged — Statement 3 is incorrect.
Only Statement 1 is correct → answer is (a): 1 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses a scope-extension trap: 'uniform across all sub-regions' converts a contextually true fact (the aquifer is large and extensive) into a false universal claim. Students in a hurry may read 'extensive aquifer system' and equate extent with uniformity. Statement 2 exploits a common misconception that pollution = industrial; the arsenic crisis in Bengal is entirely natural/geogenic, distinct from Kanpur's chromium problem.
solution.final_explanation:
The Indo-Gangetic aquifer system is vast but deeply uneven in its condition across the plain.

• Statement 1 — Correct: GRACE (Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment) satellite data show NW India (Punjab, Haryana, western UP) is losing groundwater at one of the world's fastest rates — over 4 cm/year in water table decline in some areas. This is driven by intensive paddy-wheat cultivation.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Arsenic in Bihar and West Bengal's groundwater is geogenic — it is released naturally when reducing conditions in waterlogged alluvial sediments dissolve arsenic from iron-bearing minerals. This is separate from and unrelated to industrial effluents.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The aquifer is far from uniform. The upper doab is critically overexploited; much of lower Bihar is waterlogged with high water tables. The word 'uniform' makes this categorically false.

Value Addition:
• Over 50 million people in South/Southeast Asia are exposed to geogenic arsenic — largest mass poisoning in human history.
• GRACE-FO (Follow-On) satellite continues monitoring groundwater changes globally.
• Punjab's groundwater crisis is linked to the Minimum Support Price structure incentivising paddy over less water-intensive crops.

solution.concept_anchor: Ken-Betwa link — NRLP, Panna Tiger Reserve conflict
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who associate river interlinking with water disputes may invoke the National Water Policy rather than the specific NRLP framework and Ken-Betwa's status as its first project.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a water transfer project between two Peninsular Yamuna tributaries — the Ken and the Betwa.
Eliminate (a): The Farakka Barrage transfers Ganga water to Hooghly — this is a distributary diversion, not an inter-river link between two tributaries.
Eliminate (b): The National Water Policy sets principles but is not the implementing framework for specific interlinking projects; NRLP is.
Eliminate (d): Indira Gandhi Canal diverts Rajasthan Canal water from the Beas-Sutlej — entirely unrelated to the Yamuna tributaries.
Confirm (c): Ken-Betwa is the first project under the National River Linking Project, flows through Panna Tiger Reserve, and involves NGT environmental clearance disputes — all matching the scenario.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ken-Betwa River Interlinking Project is the flagship of India's National River Linking Project (NRLP) — the first interlinking project to receive cabinet approval and move toward implementation.

Key features:
• Ken and Betwa are both right-bank tributaries of the Yamuna, originating in the Vindhyan highlands.
• The project involves building the Daudhan Dam on the Ken river and constructing a canal to transfer surplus Ken water to the water-deficient Betwa basin.
• The Ken river flows through the Panna Tiger Reserve — triggering an environmental clearance controversy and interventions by the National Green Tribunal (NGT).
• The project aims to irrigate approximately 3.6 lakh hectares in Bundelkhand (MP and UP).

Option (c) is correct as it precisely describes the first NRLP project involving the two named rivers and the Panna Tiger Reserve conflict.

Value Addition:
• NRLP was conceptualised in 1980 by the Ministry of Water Resources — it envisages 30 river links.
• Panna Tiger Reserve lost its entire tiger population by 2009 (poaching/habitat loss) before successful tiger reintroduction — the interlinking dam threatens this recovery.
• Ken joins Yamuna at Chilla (Banda district, UP); Betwa at Hamirpur (UP).

solution.concept_anchor: Gangetic geomorphic zones — Bhabar-Terai-Bhangar-Khadar sequence

statement_analysis.statement: Bhabar zone: a narrow porous gravel belt at the Himalayan foothills where surface streams disappear underground
statement_analysis.reason: Bhabar is the coarse alluvial fan zone where rivers emerging from the Himalayas lose velocity, deposit gravel, and the streams percolate underground — the description is accurate.

statement_analysis.statement: Terai zone: a waterlogged, marshy belt south of Bhabar where underground streams from the Bhabar re-emerge
statement_analysis.reason: Terai is indeed the zone of re-emergence — the impermeable clay strata south of the porous Bhabar force underground water to the surface, creating swampy conditions. This is correct.

statement_analysis.statement: Khadar soils: older alluvium found on elevated terraces, containing calcium carbonate nodules, and are less fertile than Bhangar
statement_analysis.reason: This description correctly defines Bhangar, not Khadar. Khadar is the newer, more fertile alluvium deposited by annual floods in active floodplains. The description is completely reversed.

statement_analysis.statement: The Ganga-Yamuna doab is the most fertile and densely populated inter-fluve region of the Indo-Gangetic Plain
statement_analysis.reason: The Ganga-Yamuna doab (land between two rivers) is the classic example of a productive Indian doab — agriculturally rich and among India's most densely populated plains zones.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is a strong distractor because Statements 1, 2, and 4 are all correct, and students who don't scrutinise Statement 3 carefully may count three correct items but miss that Statement 3 has Khadar and Bhangar fully reversed.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Bhabar — porous gravel, streams disappear — correct.
Verify Statement 2: Terai — waterlogged, streams re-emerge south of Bhabar — correct.
Verify Statement 3: The description given (old alluvium, elevated, kankar nodules, less fertile) applies to Bhangar, not Khadar. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 4: Ganga-Yamuna doab — most fertile doab — correct. Three of four are correct → answer is (c) Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses a complete entity-swap: every attribute listed (old alluvium, elevated terrace, kankar, less fertile) belongs to Bhangar, but the statement labels it as Khadar. Students who memorise 'Khadar and Bhangar are alluvial soil types' without drilling the specific attributes of each will miss this reversal and accept Statement 3 as plausible.
solution.final_explanation:
The Indo-Gangetic Plain is divided into four geomorphic zones from the Himalayan foothills to the delta.

| Zone | Correct Status |
|---|---|
| Bhabar | Correct — porous gravel zone |
| Terai | Correct — waterlogged, re-emergence zone |
| 'Khadar' as described | Incorrect — description fits Bhangar |
| Ganga-Yamuna doab | Correct — most fertile doab |

Three pairs are correctly described → answer is (c): Only three.

Value Addition:
• Khadar = new alluvium (newer, more fertile, flood-renewed, no kankar); Bhangar = old alluvium (elevated, less fertile, contains kankar).
• Terai zone: dense sal forests, wildlife — Jim Corbett, Dudhwa national parks sit in the Terai.
• Doab literally means 'land of two waters' (Persian: do = two, ab = water).

solution.concept_anchor: Gandak joins Ganga at Hajipur — inter-country project
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students associate the Gandak Project with Nepal and might recall that Narayani is the Nepalese name, but confuse the confluence city with Patna (which is directly opposite Hajipur across the Ganga).
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Gandak originates near Mustang, Nepal-Tibet border — not the Gangotri glacier region of Uttarakhand.
Eliminate (c): Hajipur is in Vaishali district, across the Ganga from Patna — the Gandak joins at Hajipur, not within Patna city.
Eliminate (d): Gandak is called Narayani in Nepal, not 'Karnali'. Karnali is the Nepalese name for Ghaghara.
Confirm (b): The Gandak Project is a joint India-Nepal irrigation and hydropower initiative — this is correctly stated.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (d) swaps the Nepalese name: Karnali is Ghaghara's Nepali name, while Narayani is Gandak's Nepali name. Students who know 'Himalayan tributaries have Nepal names' may confuse these — both are large Nepal-originating rivers joining the Ganga in Bihar. The Hajipur vs. Patna confusion (option c) is geographic — Hajipur is directly across the river from Patna, making it feel like the same location to an imprecise student.
solution.final_explanation:
The Gandak river is a major Himalayan tributary of the Ganga with important bilateral significance.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Gandak originates near Mustang (Nepal-Tibet border), not in the Gangotri glacier area. Gangotri feeds the Bhagirathi.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Gandak (Narayani) Project is a bilateral India-Nepal project for irrigation and hydropower — the Gandak Barrage at Tribeni Canal Head works in Nepal is a key feature.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Gandak joins the Ganga at Hajipur in Vaishali district — not at Patna. Though Hajipur is directly opposite Patna across the Ganga, they are in different districts and states (Hajipur is in Bihar's Vaishali district).
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Nepalese name for Gandak is Narayani, not Karnali. Karnali is the Nepalese name for the Ghaghara river.

Value Addition:
• Hajipur hosts the famous Sonepur Mela — Asia's largest cattle fair — at the Gandak-Ganga confluence.
• Gandak originates near Mustang district, Nepal — also famous for the ancient Lo Manthang kingdom.
• The Gandak Barrage at Balmiki Nagar (Bihar) is the main diversion structure on the Indian side.

solution.concept_anchor: Son and Narmada — same plateau, opposite flow directions
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Son originates from Amarkantak plateau and flows northeast to join Ganga; Narmada originates from the same plateau and flows west to Arabian Sea. A is correct.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — The Amarkantak plateau is indeed a drainage divide and the source of both Son and Narmada. R is correct.

Step 3: Does R explain A? — Yes. The Amarkantak plateau's topography creates opposing slopes (eastward toward Ganga basin, westward toward Arabian Sea), which is precisely why Son and Narmada flow in opposite directions from the same source area. R directly explains A.
A correct + R correct + R explains A → correct_option is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap targets students who expect assertion-reason questions to have 'both correct but unrelated' answers (Type B). Here, both A and R are true AND causally linked — a drainage divide by definition causes rivers to flow in opposite directions. Students who are primed to look for unrelated pairs may choose (b) reflexively, missing that Amarkantak as a divide directly explains the opposite flow.
solution.final_explanation:
Amarkantak plateau in Madhya Pradesh is one of India's most significant drainage divides — it separates west-flowing and east-flowing river systems.

Assertion (A): The Son and Narmada rivers both originate in the Amarkantak plateau area but drain into entirely different sea basins — Son flows northeast into the Ganga (Bay of Bengal), while Narmada flows west into the Arabian Sea. This is factually correct.

Reason (R): The Amarkantak plateau acts as a watershed (drainage divide) between the Bay of Bengal drainage (east) and the Arabian Sea drainage (west). This is also correct.

Causal relationship: A drainage divide by definition causes rivers to flow in opposite directions from a shared elevated source. Amarkantak's position and elevation explain precisely why Son and Narmada flow oppositely — R directly and causally explains A. Answer is (a).

Value Addition:
• Johilla river also originates from Amarkantak — a third river from the same plateau.
• Narmada and Tapti flow through rift valleys (graben structures) — they form estuaries, not deltas.
• Son is the second largest right-bank tributary of the Ganga — a frequently tested ranking.

solution.concept_anchor: Glaciers feeding Ganga tributaries — correct glacier-river pairing
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) swaps Chorabari to Bhagirathi, exploiting students who know 'Gangotri feeds the Ganga' but confuse which specific glacier feeds which Panch Prayag tributary.
elimination_logic: Gangotri glacier → Bhagirathi: this is universally known. A-1 is confirmed.
Chorabari/Kedarnath glacier → Mandakini: Kedarnath temple sits in the Mandakini valley; the 2013 GLOF involved Chorabari Lake above Kedarnath. B-3 is confirmed.
Pindari glacier → Pindar: the Pindar river (which joins Alaknanda at Karnaprayag) originates from the Pindari glacier — etymology confirms this. C-4 is confirmed.
Satopanth glacier → Alaknanda: Satopanth is near Badrinath, from which the Alaknanda originates. D-2 is confirmed. Full match: A-1, B-3, C-4, D-2 = option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) assigns Chorabari to Bhagirathi — a plausible-sounding swap because both Chorabari and Gangotri are Uttarakhand glaciers in the same mountain zone. Students who know Kedarnath is in the Mandakini valley but don't specifically recall that Chorabari glacier is directly above the Kedarnath temple will be confused. The Pindari → Pindar pairing requires etymology awareness that many students lack.
solution.final_explanation:
Matching Himalayan glaciers to the rivers they feed requires precision about both geography and etymology.

Correct matches:
• A (Gangotri) — 1 (Bhagirathi): Gangotri glacier in Uttarkashi district is the source of Bhagirathi, which becomes Ganga at Devprayag.
• B (Chorabari/Kedarnath) — 3 (Mandakini): Chorabari glacier sits above Kedarnath temple; the 2013 GLOF from Chorabari Lake devastated the Mandakini valley.
• C (Pindari) — 4 (Pindar): Pindari glacier in Kumaon is the etymological and hydrological source of the Pindar river, which joins Alaknanda at Karnaprayag.
• D (Satopanth) — 2 (Alaknanda): Satopanth glacier near Badrinath feeds the upper Alaknanda.

The trap pairing in options is Chorabari-Bhagirathi (wrong — Gangotri feeds Bhagirathi) and Gangotri-Alaknanda (wrong — Satopanth feeds Alaknanda).

Value Addition:
• Zemu glacier in Sikkim feeds the Teesta — it is NOT part of the Ganga system.
• The 2021 Chamoli disaster involved a rock-ice avalanche into the Rishiganga — a tributary of Alaknanda.
• Pindari glacier trek is a popular Kumaon Himalaya destination.

solution.concept_anchor: Farakka Barrage and Ganga Water Treaty — construction vs. treaty sequence
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) places the 1996 treaty before the barrage's commissioning, which students who associate 'treaty → construction' (common in dam projects) might accept.
elimination_logic: Farakka Barrage construction was completed and commissioned in 1975 — this is the earliest dateable event.
The Ganga Water Treaty (30-year treaty) between India and Bangladesh was signed in 1996 — after the barrage was operational.
The Sikkim 2023 GLOF (South Lhonak Lake) is the most recent event, though it affects the Teesta — the question uses it as a current-affairs anchor for 2023.
Correct sequence: 1975 (Farakka commissioned) → 1996 (Ganga Water Treaty) → 2023 (Sikkim GLOF) = option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal trap involves the 1996 treaty: students who know the treaty exists but confuse it with earlier interim arrangements (there were short-term agreements in 1977 and 1982/1985) may misorder the events. Option (b) places the treaty before commissioning, which is logically implausible but feels plausible to students who think 'agreements precede construction' from other project experiences.
solution.final_explanation:
Key events in India-Bangladesh water relations and Himalayan river management follow a clear chronological order:

1. Farakka Barrage commissioned (1975): Built across the Ganga in West Bengal to divert water into Hooghly and revive Kolkata Port's navigability. This immediately became a point of friction with Bangladesh.

2. Ganga Water Treaty (1996): A landmark 30-year treaty between India and Bangladesh allocating Ganga flows at Farakka during the lean season (January–May). It superseded short-term arrangements of 1977, 1982, and 1985.

3. South Lhonak GLOF, Sikkim (2023): A glacial lake outburst flood devastated the Teesta valley, breaching the Chungthang Dam — the largest hydropower project in Sikkim. This event post-dates both preceding events.

Correct sequence: Farakka commissioning → Ganga Water Treaty → Sikkim GLOF = option (c).

Value Addition:
• The 1996 Ganga Water Treaty expires in 2026 — its renewal is a current diplomatic issue.
• Farakka is located in Murshidabad district, West Bengal — just before the Bangladesh border.
• Bangladesh's Padma river (= Ganga) sees reduced flow post-Farakka — salinity ingress affects the Khulna region.

solution.concept_anchor: Left-bank vs. right-bank Ganga tributaries — Yamuna distinction
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because Gomti flows through Lucknow and students associate it with the Yamuna-adjacent UP heartland, potentially misclassifying it as a Yamuna tributary.
elimination_logic: Gomti: left-bank tributary of Ganga (joins near Ghazipur) — part of the direct Ganga system.
Ramganga: left-bank tributary of Ganga (joins near Kannauj) — part of the direct Ganga system.
Ghaghara: left-bank tributary of Ganga (joins in Saran district, Bihar) — part of the direct Ganga system.
Yamuna: the largest and longest tributary of Ganga — but it is a RIGHT-BANK tributary, whereas Gomti, Ramganga, and Ghaghara are all LEFT-BANK tributaries. Yamuna is the odd one out by bank position.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap groups Yamuna with left-bank Himalayan tributaries by emphasising 'major Ganga tributaries'. Yamuna is so prominent that students don't think of its bank position — yet it drains from the west (right bank) while Gomti, Ramganga, and Ghaghara all join from the east/north (left bank). Students who confuse bank positions or don't verify them will miss this.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests awareness of which bank of the Ganga each tributary joins from.

• Gomti — Left bank: originates from Pilibhit (UP plains), flows east, joins Ganga near Ghazipur from the left (north) bank.
• Ramganga — Left bank: originates in Pauri Garhwal (Uttarakhand), joins Ganga near Kannauj from the left (north) bank.
• Ghaghara — Left bank: originates from Tibet/Nepal, joins Ganga in Saran district (Bihar) from the left (north) bank.
• Yamuna — Right bank: originates from Yamunotri (northwest), flows parallel to Ganga for much of its length, and joins at Prayagraj from the RIGHT (south) bank.

Yamuna is the odd one out — it is a right-bank tributary, while the others are left-bank.

Value Addition:
• Right-bank Ganga tributaries (mainly Peninsular): Yamuna, Son, Damodar (via Hooghly), Chambal (via Yamuna).
• Left-bank Ganga tributaries (mainly Himalayan): Ramganga, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi, Gomti, Teesta (indirectly via Brahmaputra).
• Prayagraj (Triveni Sangam) is at the Yamuna-Ganga right-bank confluence — sacred pilgrimage site.

solution.concept_anchor: Sundarbans — UNESCO, Ramsar, shared biosphere reserve

statement_analysis.statement: The Sundarbans is recognised simultaneously as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, a Ramsar wetland, and a biosphere reserve shared between India and Bangladesh.
statement_analysis.reason: Sundarbans holds all three designations: UNESCO Natural World Heritage Site (1987), Ramsar wetland (India's portion), and a Biosphere Reserve on both sides. It is correctly described as shared between India and Bangladesh.

statement_analysis.statement: The Hooghly is the only distributary of the Ganga that is commercially navigable, and it is the easternmost distributary of the Ganga delta in India.
statement_analysis.reason: Hooghly is indeed the only commercially navigable distributary — but it is the WESTERNMOST distributary of the Ganga delta in India, not the easternmost. The scope-extension error flips the directional qualifier.

statement_analysis.statement: The main Ganga channel after crossing into Bangladesh is called the Padma, while the Brahmaputra is called the Jamuna — these two meet near Chandpur to form the Meghna.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the standard Bangladesh river nomenclature: Ganga → Padma, Brahmaputra → Jamuna. Padma and Jamuna meet near Aricha/Goalanda, and eventually the combined flow meets the Meghna near Chandpur — this is factually correct.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'All three' is a strong distractor because Statement 2 sounds authoritative — 'only navigable distributary' is true, but the trap is the directional qualifier (easternmost vs. westernmost).
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Sundarbans — UNESCO (1987), Ramsar, shared biosphere reserve — all three designations are accurate. Statement 1 is correct.

Verify Statement 2: Hooghly is the only navigable distributary — correct. But 'easternmost'? Hooghly is the WESTERNMOST distributary (it branches off near Murshidabad and flows southwest). Statement 2 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: Padma (Ganga) + Jamuna (Brahmaputra) → Meghna near Chandpur — standard Bangladesh river geography. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → answer is (b): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses a directional scope-extension: 'easternmost' replaces 'westernmost'. The Hooghly branches off the Ganga near Murshidabad in the northwest of the delta and flows southwest past Kolkata. Students who know 'Hooghly is the only navigable distributary' will focus on that fact and skim past the directional qualifier — accepting 'easternmost' without verification.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ganga delta distributary system and Bangladesh river nomenclature are high-value exam topics.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Sundarbans (Indian portion in West Bengal) is a UNESCO Natural World Heritage Site (1987), Ramsar wetland, and biosphere reserve. Bangladesh's Sundarbans is separately designated — together they form the world's largest mangrove ecosystem (~10,000 sq km).
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Hooghly is the westernmost distributary of the Indian portion of the Ganga delta — NOT the easternmost. It branches off near Farakka/Murshidabad and flows southwest through Kolkata.
• Statement 3 — Correct: In Bangladesh, Ganga = Padma; Brahmaputra = Jamuna. These merge near Aricha, and the combined river (with Meghna inputs) flows as Meghna to the Bay of Bengal near Chandpur.

Value Addition:
• Farakka Barrage (1975) diverts water into Hooghly to maintain its navigability — the primary stated purpose.
• Kolkata Port's dredging operations are perpetually challenged by Hooghly's siltation.
• Bangladesh's Sundarbans (Khulna division) is slightly larger than India's (West Bengal) portion.

solution.concept_anchor: River avulsion — antecedent drainage and lateral migration
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because the term 'superimposed drainage' sounds relevant to rivers cutting through different rock layers — students unfamiliar with the precise definition might confuse it with the Kosi's course-changing behaviour.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a river that pre-dates mountain ranges (antecedent) AND has dramatically shifted its course laterally over centuries (avulsion).
Eliminate (b): Consequent drainage develops in response to existing topography — the opposite of a river that pre-dates mountains.
Eliminate (c): Superimposed drainage involves rivers cutting through underlying rock structures — it explains gorge formation, not lateral course shifting.
Eliminate (d): Subsequent drainage develops along lines of weakness in rock — it does not explain lateral avulsion or pre-mountain-age rivers.
Confirm (a): The Kosi exhibits antecedent drainage (pre-dates Himalayas, cuts gorges) AND river avulsion (~120 km westward course shift over 200 years) — both characteristics are captured in (a).
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario combines two key geographical concepts: antecedent drainage and river avulsion.

Antecedent drainage: the river system is older than the Himalayas — as tectonic uplift occurred, the river maintained its original course and cut progressively deeper gorges through rising mountains. The Kosi originates in Nepal/Tibet and cuts through the Himalayan ranges in this manner.

River avulsion: the Kosi has one of the world's highest lateral migration rates — approximately 120 km westward over 200 years. This occurs because the Kosi carries enormous sediment loads from the Himalayas, which build up alluvial fans on the plains, causing the river to jump to a new lower-lying channel periodically.

Option (a) correctly identifies both antecedent nature AND the lateral course-shifting (avulsion) characteristic. Options (b), (c), and (d) describe different drainage patterns that do not explain either the pre-mountain age or the lateral migration of the Kosi.

Value Addition:
• Kosi's seven headstreams include the Sun Kosi, Arun, and Tamur — all meeting in Nepal.
• The Kosi barrage at Bhimnagar (Nepal) was designed partly to prevent avulsion by controlling river course.
• River avulsion is increasingly studied in the context of flood risk management in Bihar.

solution.concept_anchor: Ganga terminal point — Sagar Island, Bay of Bengal

statement_analysis.statement: The Ganga enters the Bay of Bengal at Gangasagar (Sagar Island), where it forms a braided delta shared entirely within Indian territory.
statement_analysis.reason: The Ganga-Brahmaputra delta is shared between India and Bangladesh — it is NOT entirely within Indian territory. Sagar Island is the terminal point in India, but the delta extends into Bangladesh where it is far larger.

statement_analysis.statement: Haridwar marks the point where the Ganga exits the Himalayan ranges and enters the Indo-Gangetic Plain, making it the transition from the river's mountain course to its plains course.
statement_analysis.reason: Haridwar is precisely where the Ganga exits the Shivalik hills and descends onto the plains — it is the geomorphological boundary between the upper Himalayan course and the plains course. This statement is correct.

solution.strong_distractor: b — this IS the correct answer (2 only, since only Statement 2 is correct and Statement 1 is not correct). The strong distractor to explain would be (c): students who know the delta is partly in Bangladesh but believe Sagar Island is still a correct description of the terminal point might accept Statement 1 as 'mostly correct' and choose (c) Neither instead of (b).
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: 'shared entirely within Indian territory' — the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta spans India and Bangladesh. This qualifier makes Statement 1 incorrect.
Check Statement 2: Haridwar as the mountain-to-plain transition — this is a standard, well-documented geographic fact. Statement 2 is correct.
The question asks which are NOT correct — Statement 1 is NOT correct; Statement 2 IS correct.
Answer: only Statement 1 is NOT correct → option (a): 1 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap in Statement 1 is 'shared entirely within Indian territory'. Students who correctly recall 'Sagar Island is where Ganga meets the sea' will accept that part of the statement as true and miss the critical error — that the delta is shared with Bangladesh. The phrase 'braided delta' is also distracting because the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta IS braided — making the first half of the statement sound accurate.
solution.final_explanation:
The origin and terminal points of the Ganga require precision about both the river's Indian and international extent.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Sagar Island (Gangasagar) in West Bengal is where the Ganga meets the Bay of Bengal in India — but the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta (~59,000 sq km) is shared between India and Bangladesh. Bangladesh's portion (the Padma delta) is actually the larger share. 'Entirely within Indian territory' is factually wrong.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Haridwar is the well-established entry point of the Ganga into the Indo-Gangetic Plain. Below Haridwar, the river's gradient decreases, velocity drops, and it begins to meander — characteristic of a plains river.

Only Statement 1 is NOT correct → answer is (a): 1 only.

Value Addition:
• Gangasagar Mela (Makar Sankranti) at Sagar Island — one of India's largest pilgrimages.
• The Ganga covers approximately 2,525 km from Devprayag to Sagar Island.
• Below Haridwar, the river is diverted at the Upper Ganga Canal headworks — a major irrigation infrastructure point.

statement_analysis.statement: The Ghaghara river, known as the Karnali in Nepal, originates near the Mapchachungo glacier in Tibet and is the largest tributary of the Ganga by volume of discharge.
statement_analysis.reason: Ghaghara's Tibetan/Nepal origin near Mapchachungo glacier, its Nepali name Karnali, and its status as the highest-discharge Ganga tributary are all accurately stated.

statement_analysis.statement: The 2011 draft agreement on Teesta water sharing between India and Bangladesh could not be finalised because the central government of India refused to sign it.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2011 Teesta draft agreement was not signed because West Bengal's state government (Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee) withheld consent — not because the central government refused. The central government was prepared to sign; it was a sub-federal veto by the state.

statement_analysis.statement: The Gandak Project is a joint India-Nepal initiative that includes a barrage at Bhimnagar (Nepal) for irrigation and hydropower development.
statement_analysis.reason: The Gandak Barrage at Bhimnagar (also known as Tribeni) in Nepal is the key structure of the India-Nepal Gandak Project — both the bilateral nature and the barrage location are correctly stated.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'All three' is a strong distractor because Statement 2 contains accurate background information (the 2011 agreement, the Teesta, Bangladesh) — only the attribution of refusal is wrong.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Ghaghara = Karnali in Nepal, Mapchachungo glacier, largest by discharge — all correct. Statement 1 is correct.

Verify Statement 2: The central government WAS willing to sign in 2011 — West Bengal CM Mamata Banerjee withdrew consent citing concerns about Bengal's share. The statement incorrectly attributes the refusal to the central government. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: Gandak Project, Bhimnagar barrage, India-Nepal — all correct. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → answer is (a): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses a partial-truth trap: everything about the Teesta dispute (2011 draft, India-Bangladesh, water sharing) is accurate except the critical attribution — who blocked it. West Bengal's objection (a state government withholding federal treaty consent) is a nuanced constitutional and political geography point. Students who know 'India didn't sign the Teesta treaty' without knowing the reason will accept the central government's refusal as the explanation.
solution.final_explanation:
India's water diplomacy with Nepal and Bangladesh involves distinct bilateral mechanisms and controversies.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Ghaghara (Karnali in Nepal) originates from the Mapchachungo glacier area in Tibet and flows through Nepal before entering UP/Bihar. It carries the highest volume of water among all Ganga tributaries — exceeding even the Yamuna in discharge.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The 2011 Teesta water sharing agreement between India and Bangladesh was prepared at the prime ministerial level, but CM Mamata Banerjee withdrew consent during PM Manmohan Singh's Dhaka visit, citing insufficient water allocation for West Bengal. The central government was willing; the state government blocked it.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Gandak Project (1959 India-Nepal Treaty) involves the Bhimnagar barrage and distributes irrigation water across Bihar and parts of Nepal. It is one of India's oldest bilateral water agreements with Nepal.

Value Addition:
• India has separate water treaties with Nepal (Kosi 1954, Gandak 1959, Mahakali 1996) and Bangladesh (Ganga 1996).
• Teesta treaty remains unsigned — a persistent irritant in India-Bangladesh relations.
• West Bengal's concern: the Teesta waters are critical for North Bengal's agriculture and the Teesta Barrage irrigation system.
